 Not everyone got the same 2027 Social Security bump — and no one is giving you the exact reason why. Protect your check
 Vishesh Raisinghani Thu, November 19, 2026 at 5:50 AM EST 6 min read GC=F -1.65% 
 David Goldman/ Boston Herald via Getty Images Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below. 
 You've probably seen the headline by now: Social Security is due for a 3.6% bump in 2027. 
 The "bump" is referring to the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) announced by the Social Security Administration (SSA) in mid-October. In their press release (1), the SSA mentions that the average "retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month" in 2027.

 News about each year's COLA announcement attracts a lot of attention from retirees, policymakers and advocacy groups. But what gets less attention is the fact that the SSA has two different measures of inflation for calculating your COLA. 
 Here's why the SSA has two different methodologies and how it could impact your personal benefits. 
 Two measures of inflation 
 The SSA's official COLA is linked to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (2) (CPI-W). This is a figure published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). 
 The keyword to understand this measure is "price." Simply put, CPI-W is a measure of changes in the prices of a market basket of goods and services that workers experience during a year. According to the BLS, the CPI-W rose by 3.9% (3) over the 12 months preceding September 2026. 
 However, the SSA also uses another measure known as the National Average Wage Index (4)(AWI). The BLS tracks and publishes this measure as well. 
 The keyword for this measure is "wage." Simply put, the AWI measures changes in wages during the year. In 2026, the AWI is on track to hit 4.5%, per the SSA's 2026 Trustees Report (5). That's nearly a full percentage point higher than the official COLA. 
 With two different scales at its disposal, how does the SSA decide which one applies to you? 
 It depends on your age. 
 If you're below the age of 60, you don't qualify for benefits yet, and the agency uses the AWI to index your earnings in its benefit calculation formula. In other words, how much you qualify for depends on how much money you earn and the rate of wage inflation during your career. 
 Once you reach the age of eligibility, your full benefit amount has been set. Beyond this point, your benefits climb at the rate of annual COLA. 
 Story Continues So, next year's inflation adjustment could be different for retirees and workers. But it could also be insufficient for many people in both groups. In fact, 7 out of 10 people over the age of 55 said they believe a COLA between 5% and 8% would be sufficient to offset inflation, per AARP (6). 
 That's much higher than both AWI and CPI-W, meaning that many workers and retirees might have to find their own ways to fight inflation.

 How to fight inflation 
 If the government's inflation adjustments are below your expectations, you could consider adding hard assets to protect your portfolio. 
 For instance, if you're worried about a sudden downturn in the markets eating away at your retirement portfolio, precious metals like gold are often viewed by investors as both a recession-resistant investment and hedge against inflation. 
 That's because it's not tied to any one country, currency or economy, leading investors to flock to gold — and driving prices higher — in times of economic uncertainty or geopolitical instability. 
 What's more, the precious yellow metal can't be created out of thin air or printed at will by central banks, making it an attractive alternative to fiat currencies. This inherently limited supply can help it store value in the face of inflation.

 Real estate is another option worth considering. Its appeal is straightforward: People will always need a place to live, and rental properties can produce a steady, predictable cash flow month after month. Real estate is also a popular hedge against inflation, since property values and rental income often rise alongside the cost of living.
